messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The faint, tinny melody of a lullaby drifted from a passing car, and Naren’s hands tightened on the steering wheel of his old pickup. The song, a simple tune his wife used to hum to their son, was now a landmine. He was a farmer, a man of the soil and the sun, but for the past eighteen months, since his five-year-old son, Arun, had been hospitalized with a sudden, aggressive form of meningitis, his world had shrunk to the dimensions of a single, terrible room. The event itself was a series of frozen tableaux: the frantic drive to the emergency room, the antiseptic smell, the beeping monitors, and most of all, the sight of his son’s small, limp hand, the fingers pale and blue-tinged, lying on the white hospital sheet. That image of the hand—the specific, unnatural stillness of it—was the worst part. Even now, a glimpse of his own hand in a certain light, or the way his wife’s hand rested on the kitchen counter, could trigger a sudden, vivid reliving. The memory would not just return; it would *invade*. A fragment—the beeping of a machine, the echo of a doctor’s serious tone—would crash into his present moment, and for a terrifying second, he was back there, the fear as fresh and raw as it had been that first night.

Because of this, Naren had developed a complex set of strategies to manage his life. He had come to believe that the only way to prevent these intrusions was to outrun them. He delayed sleep until two or three in the morning, staying up in the living room with the lights blazing, watching mindless television until exhaustion finally claimed him. He was certain that if he went to bed at a normal hour, the darkness and the silence would be a perfect stage for the memory to replay. The darkness itself was a trigger, so he avoided sleep to avoid the dark, and he avoided the dark to avoid the memory. This cycle meant that during the day, he was perpetually tired, his reactions slow and his mood brittle. He also began avoiding other people. The sympathetic looks from neighbors at the feed store, the well-meaning questions about Arun’s health—all of it felt like an invitation for the memory to surface. He would take the long way home from the fields, driving past the store entirely, or pretend he hadn’t seen a friend approaching on the road. He had come to believe that social interaction was a minefield, and the most dangerous trigger was a simple, kind question.

This avoidance, however, created its own problems. By staying up all night, he was often in the kitchen or the living room in the deep, quiet hours, and the sudden creak of the house settling or the hoot of an owl outside would startle him, sending a jolt of adrenaline through his body. That jolt, in turn, would bring the memory rushing back—a sudden, shapeless fragment of the hospital room’s fear. The maladaptive strategy of staying awake actually made the triggers more potent, because his exhausted mind was more vulnerable to them. He found himself jumping at the sound of his own footsteps on the porch, his heart hammering. The more he tried to control his environment, the more unpredictable it seemed.

The memory itself felt present, not past. When he thought of Arun’s hand, it was not a recollection; it was a re-experiencing. He could feel the cold, smooth texture of the hospital linoleum under his shoes, hear the hiss of the oxygen machine. This quality of the memory made him terrified of any sensory reminder. A song on the radio, especially the lullaby, could trigger a full reliving event, where he would feel his throat tighten and his eyes sting with tears he had not shed in years. The memory was a predator, and the triggers were its scent. He had learned to be hypervigilant, scanning his environment for any potential threat—a song, a shadow, a particular shade of pale skin. He was certain that if he could just control his surroundings perfectly, he could keep the memory at bay.

The breaking point came on a Tuesday. He was driving back from the feed store, having successfully avoided everyone, when a song from a nearby house drifted through his open window. It was the same lullaby. For a full ten seconds, he was not on the rural road; he was in the hospital room, watching the doctor’s lips move without hearing the words, the world reduced to the terrifying stillness of his son’s hand. He had to pull over, his hands shaking, his breath coming in ragged gasps. That night, he did not even try to sleep. He sat in the dark of his own living room, which he had previously avoided, because he was too exhausted to care. The next morning, his wife found him staring at the wall, and for the first time, he spoke the words aloud: “I can’t keep doing this.” He was terrified that the memory was not a thing of the past, but a permanent, present threat, and that his own mind had become a place he could no longer safely inhabit. He needed to find a way to make the past stay in the past, to stop the fragments from hijacking his present, and most of all, to be able to look at his own hands without seeing his son’s.
